intro: In this lesson you'll describe people, places and things: a red car, a busy day, a very hot afternoon. An adjective is a describing word (red, busy, hot); a noun is the name of a thing, person or place (car, day, Rina). In English the adjective comes before the noun, and after a person or thing you need am, is or are. Warm-up: describe your phone in two words, like 'It's new.'
teachingNotes: Indonesian puts the adjective after the noun (mobil merah); English puts it before (a red car). Common error: *'a car red'.
a/an and plurals: a/an goes before the adjective and follows the adjective's first sound (an old house, a new phone). Adjectives never take -s: two big bags, not *'two bigs bags'.

a/an looks at the very next word, so it can change when very comes in: an old house but a very old house, an expensive car but a very expensive car. Say this explicitly; learners who know 'an before a vowel sound' are surprised by 'a very expensive'.

When the adjective comes after the person or thing, English needs be: She's tired, not *'She tired'. No 'a' before an adjective on its own: *'She is a tired'. The negative (isn't / aren't) is already known from a1-to-be.

Why be: an Indonesian sentence like 'Rina sibuk' is complete, but an English sentence always needs a verb; with no action, am/is/are does that job. Explain the jargon (adjective = kata sifat, noun = kata benda, verb = kata kerja/action word) in plain words the first time; don't assume the learner knows it. Also: English needs 'it' in 'I really like it' even though Indonesian says just 'Saya suka sekali'.

very and really go before the adjective (very hot, really cheap, a very small room). Indonesian 'sekali' comes after (panas sekali), so learners may say *'hot very'. Only really goes before a verb: I really like it, not *'I very like it'.

Limits: no comparatives or superlatives (bigger, the biggest), no adjective order with three adjectives, no -ed/-ing adjectives, no past or future. Use verbs only with I/you/we/they (I like, we have); third-person -s isn't in this lesson's prerequisites. Avoid 'very' with strong adjectives like delicious or amazing.

keyPoints.title: Adjective before the noun
keyPoints.explanation: An adjective is a describing word (red, big, cheap). In English it comes before the noun (the thing): a red car (mobil merah). a/an goes before the adjective and follows the sound of the very next word. The adjective never takes -s; only the noun does: two big bags.

keyPoints.title: be + adjective
keyPoints.explanation: After a person or thing, use am/is/are + adjective: She's tired (She's = She is). Indonesian 'Dia capek' has no verb, but an English sentence always needs one, and am/is/are does that job. Don't drop be, and don't put 'a' before the adjective alone: a means 'one (thing)' and needs a noun.

keyPoints.title: very and really
keyPoints.explanation: Put very or really before the adjective to make it stronger: very hot, really cheap. Before a verb (an action word like like), use really, not very: I really like it. 'very much' is different: it goes at the end, I like it very much.

guidedPractice.hint: The colour comes first in English.

guidedPractice.hint: a/an looks at the very next word. Say 'old' out loud: it starts with an 'o' sound (a vowel sound).

Make it stronger with very: The bag is cheap.
guidedPractice.hint: very goes right before the describing word (cheap).

independentPractice.prompt: Complete with very or really: I ___ like Bandung.
independentPractice.hint: like is an action word (a verb), not a describing word. Only really can go before a verb.

independentPractice.prompt: Make it plural: a big box → two ___
independentPractice.hint: The describing word (big) never changes. Only the thing changes: box → boxes (after x, add -es, not just -s).

assessment.prompt: Put the words in order: phone / I / new / a / have
assessment.rubric: Correct: I have a new phone. 'I have a phone new' = 30 (adjective after the noun).

assessment.prompt: Correct the mistake: It's a shirt blue.
assessment.rubric: Correct: It's a blue shirt. The adjective goes before the noun. 'It's blue shirt' (no a) = 70.

assessment.prompt: Correct the mistake: My sister tired today.
assessment.rubric: Correct: My sister is / My sister's tired today. Must add is. 'My sister is a tired today' = 40. 'My sister are tired' = 40.
Correct: The hotel is cheap (or inexpensive). Missing is ('The hotel cheap') = 30. 'The hotel is a cheap' = 40.

acceptableAnswers: we really like the new teacher

assessment.rubric: Correct: We really like the new teacher. (We like the new teacher very much / a lot is also correct.) Keeping 'very like' = 0.

assessment.prompt: Translate into English: Jakarta sangat panas.
assessment.rubric: Correct: Jakarta is very / really hot. 'Jakarta is hot very' = 40. Missing is = 40. 'Jakarta is so hot' = 80.

blocks.text: **Adjectives** are describing words: **big, small, new, old, cheap, expensive**. A **noun** is the name of a thing, person or place: *car, market, bike, Rina*. In Indonesian the adjective comes **after** the noun (*mobil merah*). In English it comes **before**: **a red car**.

id.text: **Kata sifat** (adjective) adalah kata yang menjelaskan orang, tempat atau benda: **big, small, new, old, cheap, expensive**. **Kata benda** (noun) adalah nama benda, orang atau tempat: *car, market, bike, Rina*. Dalam bahasa Indonesia kata sifat ada **setelah** kata benda (*mobil merah*). Dalam bahasa Inggris kata sifat ada **sebelum** kata benda: **a red car**.

rows.id: sepeda tua (*an*, karena *old* diawali bunyi 'o', bunyi vokal)
rows.note: an: old starts with an 'o' sound

rows.id: dua kucing putih (yang diberi -s hanya *cats*, bukan *white*)

blocks.text: **a/an** goes before the adjective and looks at the sound of the **very next word**: **a** new bag, **an** old bag. Adjectives never take **-s**: two **big bags**, not 'two bigs bags'. Why? In English only the **noun** shows 'more than one'. The describing word stays the same, like in Indonesian (*dua tas besar*: *besar* doesn't change either).

id.text: **a/an** ada sebelum kata sifat dan melihat bunyi **kata tepat sesudahnya**: **a** new bag, **an** old bag. Kata sifat tidak pernah diberi **-s**: two **big bags**, bukan 'two bigs bags'. Kenapa? Dalam bahasa Inggris, yang menunjukkan 'lebih dari satu' hanya **kata bendanya**. Kata sifatnya tetap, sama seperti bahasa Indonesia (*dua tas besar*: *besar* juga tidak berubah).

blocks.explain: The adjective cheap goes before the noun bag, and it never takes -s.

id.explain: Kata sifat cheap ada sebelum kata benda bag, dan tidak pernah diberi -s.

blocks.text: An adjective can also come **after** the person or thing. Then English needs **am, is** or **are**: *Dia capek* = **She's tired** (She's = She **is**), never 'She tired'. Why? In Indonesian *Dia capek* is a complete sentence. In English every sentence needs a verb, and when there's no action, **am / is / are** does that job. Use the negative you already know: **The bus isn't full.**

id.text: Kata sifat juga bisa ada **setelah** orang atau benda. Dalam hal ini bahasa Inggris butuh **am, is** atau **are**: *Dia capek* = **She's tired** (She's = She **is**), bukan 'She tired'. Kenapa? Dalam bahasa Indonesia *Dia capek* sudah kalimat lengkap. Dalam bahasa Inggris setiap kalimat butuh kata kerja, dan kalau tidak ada kegiatan, **am / is / are** yang mengisi tempat itu. Pakai bentuk negatif yang sudah kamu tahu: **The bus isn't full.**

blocks.text: Don't put **a** before an adjective on its own: **She is tired**, not 'She is a tired'. **a** means 'one (thing or person)', so it needs a noun after it: **She is a tired teacher.**

id.text: Jangan taruh **a** sebelum kata sifat yang berdiri sendiri: **She is tired**, bukan 'She is a tired'. **a** artinya 'satu (benda atau orang)', jadi harus ada kata benda sesudahnya: **She is a tired teacher.**

blocks.explain: My phone = it (one thing), so we use is: My phone is old.

id.explain: My phone = it (satu benda), jadi pakai is: My phone is old.

blocks.text: To make an adjective stronger, put **very** or **really** right **before** it: **very cold, really cheap**. With a noun, the order is **a + very + adjective + noun**: **a very small room**. Indonesian *sekali* comes after (*panas sekali*), but **very** comes before the describing word.

id.text: Untuk menguatkan kata sifat, taruh **very** atau **really** tepat **sebelum** kata sifat: **very cold, really cheap**. Kalau ada kata benda, urutannya **a + very + kata sifat + kata benda**: **a very small room**. *Sekali* dalam bahasa Indonesia ada di belakang (*panas sekali*), tapi **very** ada di depan kata sifatnya.

rows.id: Saya suka sekali lagu ini. (*like* = kata kerja, jadi pakai *really*)

blocks.text: Only **really** can go before a verb (an action word like *like*): **I really like it.** 'I very like it' is wrong, because **very** only makes describing words stronger. You can also say **I like it very much**: **very much** is a fixed pair that goes at the **end**. And English needs **it**: *Saya suka sekali* = **I really like it**, not 'I really like'.

id.text: Hanya **really** yang bisa ada sebelum kata kerja (kata kegiatan seperti *like*): **I really like it.** 'I very like it' salah, karena **very** hanya menguatkan kata sifat. Kamu juga bisa bilang **I like it very much**: **very much** adalah pasangan tetap yang ada di **akhir** kalimat. Dan bahasa Inggris butuh **it**: *Saya suka sekali* = **I really like it**, bukan 'I really like'.

blocks.text: **a or an with very?** a/an always looks at the **very next word**. When **very** comes in, the next word is *very* (a 'v' sound), so it's **a**: **an** old house → **a very** old house, **an** easy test → **a very** easy test.

id.text: **a atau an kalau ada very?** a/an selalu melihat **kata tepat sesudahnya**. Kalau ada **very**, kata sesudahnya adalah *very* (bunyi 'v'), jadi pakai **a**: **an** old house → **a very** old house, **an** easy test → **a very** easy test.

blocks.explain: very goes right before the adjective: very big.

id.explain: very ada tepat sebelum kata sifat: very big.

id.title: Lebih kuat dengan very dan really

blocks.text: Many adjectives come in opposite pairs. Learn them together, then describe your room, your city or your office: *My office is small but very clean.*

id.text: Banyak kata sifat punya pasangan lawan kata. Pelajari bersama-sama, lalu deskripsikan kamarmu, kotamu atau kantormu: *My office is small but very clean.*

blocks.text: **old** is for people and things, but the opposite changes: for things it's **new** (an old phone – a new phone), for people it's **young** (an old man – a young man). In Indonesian these are different words too: *lama/baru* for things, *tua/muda* for people.

id.text: **old** dipakai untuk orang dan benda, tapi lawan katanya berbeda: untuk benda **new** (an old phone = ponsel lama – a new phone = ponsel baru), untuk orang **young** (an old man = pria tua – a young man = pria muda). Dalam bahasa Indonesia juga beda kata: *lama/baru* untuk benda, *tua/muda* untuk orang.

suggestedQuestions: Why does the adjective come before the noun in English?
When do I need is or are with an adjective?
What's the difference between very and really?

id.intro: Di pelajaran ini kamu akan mendeskripsikan orang, tempat dan benda: a red car, a busy day, a very hot afternoon. Kata sifat (adjective) adalah kata yang menjelaskan (red, busy, hot); kata benda (noun) adalah nama benda, orang atau tempat (car, day, Rina). Dalam bahasa Inggris kata sifat ada sebelum kata benda, dan setelah orang atau benda kamu butuh am, is atau are. Pemanasan: deskripsikan ponselmu dengan dua kata, misalnya 'It's new.'
